claims.text: The target alloy is a quaternary equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloy.
The target alloy has a single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
The target quaternary alloy is compositionally similar to CoCrFeMnNi.
The target alloy may be compositionally similar to an Al-free variant of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5.
Vacuum arc melting followed by annealing can produce a homogeneous initial state for the proposed alloy.
A high-temperature strength plateau occurs between approximately 873 K and 1073 K.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate between 873 K and 1073 K.
Yielding in the target FCC alloy is dislocation-based rather than caused by a deformation-induced phase transformation.
Edge dislocations can control strength in refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
Highly mobile edge dislocations undergo thermal super-jogging and are the primary carriers of plasticity.
At high homologous temperatures, activation barriers for dislocation climb and cross-slip become sufficiently low to change the rate-limiting yielding process.
The rate-limiting process changes from thermally activated screw-dislocation kink-pair formation to athermic edge-dislocation motion or drag.
A transition to athermic edge-dislocation-controlled motion causes a plateau in the strain-rate dependence of yield strength.
No deformation twins or deformation-induced HCP or BCC phases will form during high-temperature tension.
Standard thermally activated dislocation-glide models predict a strong positive logarithmic dependence of yield strength on strain rate at all temperatures.
TRIP and TWIP mechanisms generally exhibit distinct strain-rate dependence or characteristic microstructural evolution.
A sufficiently high valence electron concentration supports FCC phase stability in the target alloy.
The hypothesis does not apply to alloys containing significant BCC or B2 secondary phases or to alloys prone to deformation-induced transformation.
Additions such as C or Al can induce HCP or BCC phases in relevant high-entropy alloys.
The proposed dominance of edge dislocations in the FCC target is extrapolated from evidence on BCC refractory alloys and may not transfer directly.

contradictions.description: The target is described as quaternary and equiatomic, but CoCrFeMnNi is a five-element system and NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a six-element, non-equiatomic system.

The initial-state description invokes a refractory NbTaHfTiZrV0.5-type system as an analogue, while the boundary explicitly excludes alloys with significant BCC/B2 character; the cited refractory systems used for the mechanism are BCC rather than FCC.

The hypothesis asserts a strain-rate-insensitive plateau, whereas the cited and described 'high-temperature plateau' is a plateau of strength versus temperature. These are distinct dependencies and are conflated in the predicted outcome.
